newsitem.title: USA: IMF's Mussa--room for possible Europe rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: IMF's Mussa--room for possible Europe rate cuts.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund official said on Wednesday that he saw possible room for a somewhat easier monetary policy in Europe.
"I am among those who have thought the balance of risk over the last year or so did argue in the direction of a somewhat easier stance," IMF chief economist Michael Mussa told a news conference.
However, Mussa said he did not want to exaggerate the economic impact of a further half-percentage point drop in European rates, noting that monetary conditions there are already very accomodative.
"I believe that monetary policy (in Europe) will remain ... reasonably accommodative over the next couple of years" in the runup to the formation of the new European Central Bank, Mussa said.
He said he expects the new central bank to pursue a monetary stance similar to that of Germany's Bundesbank and perhaps be a bit less tolerant of inflation than the U.S. Federal Reserve.
"The U.S. Federal Reserve seems, with (inflation) at three percent or a little bit under, not to want to push too hard to drive it down," Mussa said.
Mussa spoke to reporters following a two-day conference at the IMF on European monetary union.
He said that participants in the conference, which included academics, IMF and government officials, agreed in their belief that EMU will be launched eventually, probably on time on January 1, 1999.
There was also general agreement that Europe's new currency, the euro, will be relatively strong and will become a key rival to the dollar, he said.

For his part, Mussa said he does not see the euro behaving in a much different way on currency markets than Germany's mark does now, with its level determined by interest rate spreads and economic growth differentials.
Mussa added that Europe has the potential now for a "meaningful" cyclical economic recovery.
"We can expect ... a significant pickup in growth in Europe during the course of 1997," Mussa said.
